title: fd
description: fd — a simple, fast, and user-friendly alternative to the classic Unix find command, written in Rust. Respects .gitignore by default, uses sensible defaults, and offers a friendlier syntax for the common cases while still supporting parallel command execution.

Getting Started.Getting Started:
`fd` is a single self-contained binary. No configuration is needed to get
useful, ignore-aware defaults out of the box.

## Current version

The latest stable release is **fd 10.5.0** (August 2026). Recent notable
additions worth knowing about if you're used to an older `fd`:

- `--exact` (10.5.0) — match the entire filename literally, no substring/regex.
- `--ignore-parent` (10.5.0) — override an inherited `--no-ignore-parent`.
- `--ignore-contain` (10.4.0) — skip directories containing a named marker file (e.g. `CACHEDIR.TAG`).
- `--hyperlink` (10.2.0) — emit OSC 8 terminal hyperlinks in output.
- `--format` (10.1.0) — template-based output, similar syntax to `--exec`.
- Date filters (`--changed-within`/`--changed-before`) switched to the `jiff`
  crate in 10.3.0 — `M` alone no longer means "month" (use `mo`/`mos`/`month`
  to avoid ambiguity with minutes).

## Install on Arch Linux

```bash
sudo pacman -S fd
```

Arch's `extra` repository tracks upstream releases closely.

## Install elsewhere

```bash
# macOS
brew install fd

# Debian/Ubuntu (binary is named fdfind due to a name clash; recent
# packages also ship an `fd` symlink)
sudo apt install fd-find

# Via cargo
cargo install fd-find
```

## Check your version

```bash
fd --version
```

## Your first search

```bash
fd pattern
```

Run with no path, `fd` searches the current directory recursively for
filenames matching `pattern` as a substring (case-insensitively by
default), automatically skipping anything `.gitignore` excludes, hidden
files, and the `.git` directory itself.

```bash
fd config          # any file/dir with "config" in its name
fd '\.dart$'        # regex mode: files ending in .dart
fd . lib/           # "." matches everything; list all files under lib/
```

See [Core Concepts](/fd/core-concepts/) for how `fd`'s ignore-aware
defaults and pattern matching differ from `find`.
Getting Started.Core Concepts:
## The ignore-aware default

Like ripgrep (same author, shared underlying `ignore` crate), `fd`
automatically skips, with zero configuration:

- Anything matched by `.gitignore` (at any level) or a local `.ignore` file.
- Hidden files and directories (dotfiles), unless `-H`/`--hidden` is passed.
- The `.git` directory itself.

As of fd 9.0.0 (and confirmed unchanged through 10.5.0), passing
`--hidden` does **not** automatically re-include `.git` — `.git/` stays
excluded unless you also pass `--no-ignore` or `--no-ignore-vcs`. This
reverted an earlier, differently-behaving version, so don't trust older
blog posts that say otherwise.

```bash
fd -H "config"                       # search hidden files, .git still excluded
fd -H --no-ignore-vcs "config"       # search hidden files, .git included too
fd -I "config"                       # -I / --no-ignore: bypass .gitignore entirely
```

## Pattern matching modes

| Mode | Flag | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Regex (default) | *(none)* | Pattern is a Rust-regex substring match against the filename. |
| Glob | `-g` / `--glob` | Pattern is a glob (`*.rs`) instead of regex. |
| Exact | `-x` (short for `--exec`, unrelated) / see note | See `--exact` below for literal matching. |
| Fixed string | `--fixed-strings` | No regex/glob interpretation, literal substring. |

```bash
fd -g '*.dart' lib/         # glob mode
fd --exact 'main.dart'      # 10.5.0+: entire filename must equal this, literally
```

Unlike `grep`/`ripgrep`, by default `fd` matches against just the
**filename**, not the full path. Use `-p`/`--full-path` to match against
the entire path instead:

```bash
fd -p 'src/.*\.dart$'
```

## Exit status

`0` if at least one match was found, `1` otherwise — same convention as
`grep`/`ripgrep`, usable for scripting.

## How fd differs from find, at a glance

| | `find` | `fd` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Default target | Path (any part) | Filename only (unless `-p`) |
| Ignores `.gitignore` | No | Yes, by default |
| Skips hidden files | No | Yes, by default |
| Parallel traversal | No | Yes |
| Regex support | `-regex` (full path, various dialects) | Built-in, filename by default |
| Color output | No | Yes, by default in a terminal |
| Syntax | `find PATH -name PATTERN` | `fd PATTERN PATH` |

See [Pattern Matching & Filters](/fd/pattern-matching-filters/) for the
full filter flag set and [Executing Commands](/fd/executing-commands/) for
`--exec`/`--exec-batch`.

Guides.Pattern Matching & Filters:
## Type filters

```bash
fd -t f "main"          # files only
fd -t d "src"           # directories only
fd -t l                 # symlinks only
fd -t x                 # executable files
fd -t e                 # empty files or directories
```

`-t`/`--type` accepts: `f` (file), `d` (directory), `l` (symlink),
`x` (executable), `e` (empty), and (added recently) `dir` as an alias for
`directory`, plus character/block device types on platforms that expose
them.

## Extension filters

```bash
fd -e dart              # only .dart files
fd -e dart -e yaml       # .dart OR .yaml
```

## Glob vs regex vs exact vs fixed-string

```bash
fd 'te?t'                    # regex: "te" + any single char + "t"
fd -g '*.g.dart'              # glob: generated Dart files
fd --fixed-strings '[draft]'  # literal, no regex/glob metachars interpreted
fd --exact 'pubspec.yaml'     # 10.5.0+: filename must equal this exactly
```

## Size and depth filters

```bash
fd -S +10M                   # files larger than 10 MB
fd -S -1k                    # files smaller than 1 KB
fd --min-depth 2 --max-depth 3
fd -d 2                       # shorthand for --max-depth 2
```

## Time filters

Since fd 10.3.0, time-duration parsing uses the `jiff` crate. This changed
how bare `M` is interpreted — it's no longer "month" (to avoid ambiguity
with minutes); spell out `mo`/`mos`/`month`/`months` instead.

```bash
fd --changed-within 1d         # modified in the last day
fd --changed-within 2h         # modified in the last 2 hours
fd --changed-within 3mo        # modified in the last 3 months (NOT "3M")
fd --changed-before 2025-01-01
fd --changed-before @1700000000  # Unix timestamp, GNU-date style
```

## Owner filters (Unix)

```bash
fd --owner root              # owned by user "root"
fd --owner :staff            # owned by group "staff"
fd --owner root:staff        # both
```

## Ignoring directories that contain a marker file

```bash
fd --ignore-contain CACHEDIR.TAG "*.log"
```

Added in fd 10.4.0 — skips any directory tree containing a file with that
exact name, the same convention `CACHEDIR.TAG` uses to mark cache
directories that backup tools should skip.

## Combining filters

Filters combine with implicit AND:

```bash
fd -e dart -t f -S +5k --changed-within 1w
```

See [Executing Commands](/fd/executing-commands/) for running commands on
the results.
Guides.Executing Commands:
## `-x` / `--exec`: run a command per result

```bash
fd -e dart -x dart format
```

Runs `dart format <file>` once **per matching file**. `{}` is available as
an explicit placeholder if you need the match somewhere other than the end
of the command:

```bash
fd -e dart -x mv {} {}.bak
```

Other placeholders:

| Placeholder | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `{}` | Full path of the match. |
| `{.}` | Path without file extension. |
| `{/}` | Basename only. |
| `{//}` | Parent directory. |
| `{/.}` | Basename without extension. |

```bash
fd -e dart -x mv {} {.}.old.dart
```

## `-X` / `--exec-batch`: run a command once with all results

```bash
fd -e dart -X wc -l
```

This runs `wc -l file1.dart file2.dart file3.dart ...` as a single
invocation, rather than once per file — much faster for commands that
accept multiple arguments.

## `--format`: template-based output

Added in fd 10.1.0, similar placeholder syntax to `--exec` but for
formatting stdout instead of building a command:

```bash
fd -e dart --format '{/}: {}'
```

## Note on `--print0`

```bash
fd -e dart --print0 | xargs -0 dart format
```

`--print0` NUL-separates results for safe piping into `xargs -0`, handling
filenames with spaces or newlines correctly — the same idiom used with
`find -print0`. Since fd 10.4.0, `--print0` combined with `--exec` places
the NUL between each *set* of commands run, not between every individual
invocation.

See [Recipes](/fd/recipes/) for these assembled into full workflows.
Guides.Recipes:
## Find and format every Dart file

```bash
fd -e dart -x dart format
```

## Delete all build artifacts (dry run first!)

```bash
fd -t d -H '^(build|\.dart_tool)$' -X echo rm -rf   # preview
fd -t d -H '^(build|\.dart_tool)$' -X rm -rf        # actually delete
```

## List files modified in the last hour, newest look-and-feel

```bash
fd --changed-within 1h -l
```

`-l`/`--list-details` shows `ls -l`-style output (permissions, size,
modified time) instead of just the path.

## Count lines across all Dart source files

```bash
fd -e dart -X wc -l
```

## Find large files anywhere in a project, ignoring .gitignore

```bash
fd -I -S +50M
```

## Search including dotfiles but excluding .git

```bash
fd -H --no-ignore-vcs -E .git "TODO"
```

`-E`/`--exclude` adds an extra glob exclusion on top of whatever ignore
rules already apply.

## Rename all matches with a shell command

```bash
fd -e jpeg -x mv {} {.}.jpg
```

## Generate a file listing for another tool

```bash
fd -e dart --print0 lib/ > /dev/null   # sanity check pattern first
fd -e dart -0 lib/ | xargs -0 grep -l "TODO"
```

## Use fd as a faster find-by-name in scripts

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
if fd -q "pubspec.yaml" .; then
  echo "Dart project detected"
fi
```

`-q`/`--quiet` suppresses output; combine with the exit status like `grep -q`.

Project.FAQ:
### Why isn't `fd` finding a file I know exists?

Almost always the ignore-aware defaults. Try progressively:

```bash
fd -H pattern              # include hidden files (still skips .git)
fd -H --no-ignore-vcs pattern   # also include .git
fd -I pattern               # bypass .gitignore entirely
```

### Does `fd` search full paths or just filenames?

Filenames only, by default. Use `-p`/`--full-path` to match the pattern
against the entire path instead.

### Is `fd`'s pattern a regex by default?

Yes — unlike shell globbing, `fd PATTERN` treats `PATTERN` as a regular
expression matched against the filename. Use `-g`/`--glob` if you want
shell-glob syntax (`*.dart`) instead, or `--fixed-strings` for a literal
substring with no special-character interpretation.

### What's the difference between `--exec` and `--exec-batch`?

`-x`/`--exec` runs the given command once *per matching file*.
`-X`/`--exec-batch` runs the command *once*, with every match passed as
arguments — much faster when the underlying tool supports multiple file
arguments (like `wc`, `dart format`, `grep -l`, etc.).

### Why did `--changed-within 3M` stop meaning "3 months"?

fd 10.3.0 switched its date-duration parser to the `jiff` crate. To avoid
`M` (month) being confused with `m`/minutes in case-insensitive contexts,
bare `M` was dropped; spell out `mo`, `mos`, `month`, or `months` instead.

### Is there a Debian/Ubuntu naming quirk?

Yes — the Debian/Ubuntu package installs the binary as `fdfind` because
the name `fd` was already taken by an unrelated package. Recent `.deb`
releases also include an `fdfind → fd` symlink so both names work; check
your package version if `fd` isn't found after installing.
